message.content:
Under Read Committed isolation, a SQL statement sees changes committed by other transactions after the statement begins, but within a single statement, the data is consistent and "frozen" [1]. In contrast, under Repeatable Read isolation, a transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the data throughout its duration and will not observe changes from concurrently committing transactions [1]. 

The two backup components needed for point-in-time recovery in PostgreSQL are a physical base backup and continuous WAL archiving [2][4][5].

sources.title: Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ

passages.text: One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.

The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.

In READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.

However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.

In the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions.

sources.title: PostgreSQL Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery with pgBackRest

passages.text:
This article is part of a series on PostgreSQL WAL.

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.

passages.heading: How WAL Enables Point-in-Time Recovery
passages.text:
Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.

passages.heading: Final Thoughts
passages.text:
Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows.

✅ Step 9: Give the full security permission for user in folder "C:\PostgreSQL\data" and Start PostgreSQL on Recovery Server

`net start postgresql-x64-17`        

          Check service status in services.msc or Event Viewer.

✅ Step 10: Verify Recovery Status

In SQL Shell (psql):

`\c chirags_db1`        

          `\dt`        

          `SELECT * FROM users;`        

          `SELECT * FROM accounts;`        

          If you see both users and accounts tables, PITR was successful.

✅ Step 11: Exit Read-Only Mode

`SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();`        

          🎉 Final Output Validation

`SELECT * FROM users;`        

          `SELECT * FROM accounts;`        

          `SELECT now();`        

          ✅ Summary

Plenty of Kubernetes backup content treats point-in-time recovery like a fancy snapshot feature. That is not how PostgreSQL works.

PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, or PITR, is a recovery model built from two things together:

- a physical base backup
- a continuous archive of write-ahead log, or WAL, files

The current PostgreSQL documentation is explicit about this. PITR combines a file-system-level backup with archived WAL, then replays WAL until the target time you want to restore to. In other words, snapshots can help, but snapshots alone are not PITR.

That distinction matters even more on Kubernetes, where teams often have:

- CSI snapshots
- operator-managed backups
- object-store retention
- multiple PVCs
- automation that looks reassuring until the first real restore

passages.heading: A Practical PITR Design for Kubernetes
passages.text:
If you want a design that is operationally sane, keep it simple:

- take regular physical base backups
- archive WAL continuously to object storage
- use snapshots to accelerate recovery when your storage stack supports them
- restore into a new cluster, then validate before promotion

That avoids two common traps:

- treating snapshots as the whole disaster-recovery plan
- overcomplicating recovery with too many one-off scripts and manual steps

If your operator supports it, snapshot-based recovery can shorten the time needed to rehydrate large datasets. CloudNativePG, for example, supports restoring from a `VolumeSnapshot` and then applying archived WAL to reach the target time. It also warns that if you use separate WAL storage, that snapshot must be included too.

passages.heading: What does PostgreSQL PITR on Kubernetes actually require?
passages.text: At minimum, you need a recoverable base backup, continuous WAL archiving, and a tested restore workflow that can recover to a specific target time or restore point.

sources.title: PostgreSQL Point-in-Time Recovery with WAL Archiving | Stack Harbor

passages.text: Point-in-time recovery (PITR) lets you restore a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster to any exact moment — the instant before a bad `DELETE`, not just last night’s snapshot. It rests on two pieces: a physical base backup taken with `pg_basebackup`, and a continuous stream of write-ahead log (WAL) segments shipped off the server by `archive_command`. To recover, you lay down the base backup, point `restore_command` at the WAL archive, set `recovery_target_time` to the moment you want, drop a `recovery.signal` file, and start the server. It replays WAL forward from the backup until it reaches your target, then stops. On PostgreSQL 15, 16, and 17 the old `recovery.conf` is gone — recovery settings live in `postgresql.auto.conf` and the presence of `recovery.signal` is what puts the server into recovery mode. The configuration is a few lines; the part that actually saves you is rehearsing the restore before you need it.

passages.heading: Step-by-step
passages.text:
```
LOG:  starting point-in-time recovery to 2026-07-21 14:19:55-04
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000004" from archive
LOG:  recovery stopping before commit of transaction 1234, time 2026-07-21 14:19:56.02-04
LOG:  recovery has paused
HINT:  Execute pg_wal_replay_resume() to promote.
```
**10. Inspect, then promote.** Connect and check the data (see the next section). When satisfied, end recovery and open the cluster read-write.

`SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();`
The server finishes on a new timeline and begins accepting writes. `pg_promote()` is the equivalent when you want to force the end immediately.

passages.heading: When this is the wrong approach
passages.text:
For the authoritative reference on every parameter, see the PostgreSQL manual on Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery and the recovery target settings.

If this is the kind of work you’d rather never own again, it’s the daily job of Managed Cloud Ops — book an infrastructure review.

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}

{"url": "https://cybertec-postgresql.com/en/transactions-in-postgresql-read-committed-vs-repeatable-read", "title": "Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ", "date": "2018-11-28", "passages": ["One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.", "The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.", "Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.", "Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows."]}

The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.", "The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time

Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.", "Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

That is not how PostgreSQL works.

PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, or PITR, is a recovery model built from two things together:

- a physical base backup
- a continuous archive of write-ahead log, or WAL, files

The current PostgreSQL documentation is explicit about this. PITR combines a file-system-level backup with archived WAL, then replays WAL until the target time you want to restore to. In other words, snapshots can help, but snapshots alone are not PITR.

That distinction matters even more on Kubernetes, where teams often have:

- CSI snapshots
- operator-managed backups
- object-store retention
- multiple PVCs
- automation that looks reassuring until the first real restore", "If you want a design that is operationally sane, keep it simple:

- take regular physical base backups
- archive WAL continuously to object storage
- use snapshots to accelerate recovery when your storage stack supports them
- restore into a new cluster, then validate before promotion

That avoids two common traps:

- treating snapshots as the whole disaster-recovery plan
- overcomplicating recovery with too many one-off scripts and manual steps

If your operator supports it, snapshot-based recovery can shorten the time needed to rehydrate large datasets. CloudNativePG, for example, supports restoring from a `VolumeSnapshot` and then applying archived WAL to reach the target time. It also warns that if you use separate WAL storage, that snapshot must be included too.", "At minimum, you need a recoverable base backup, continuous WAL archiving, and a tested restore workflow that can recover to a specific target time or restore point."]}

<source id="1" title="Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ" site="CYBERTEC PostgreSQL | Services & Support" published="2018-11-28">
Citation label: [1]

One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.

The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.

In READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.

However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.

In the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions.
</source>

This article is part of a series on PostgreSQL WAL.

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.

Section: How WAL Enables Point-in-Time Recovery
Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.

Section: Final Thoughts
Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows.
</source>

Plenty of Kubernetes backup content treats point-in-time recovery like a fancy snapshot feature. That is not how PostgreSQL works.

PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, or PITR, is a recovery model built from two things together:

- a physical base backup
- a continuous archive of write-ahead log, or WAL, files

The current PostgreSQL documentation is explicit about this. PITR combines a file-system-level backup with archived WAL, then replays WAL until the target time you want to restore to. In other words, snapshots can help, but snapshots alone are not PITR.

That distinction matters even more on Kubernetes, where teams often have:

- CSI snapshots
- operator-managed backups
- object-store retention
- multiple PVCs
- automation that looks reassuring until the first real restore

Section: A Practical PITR Design for Kubernetes
If you want a design that is operationally sane, keep it simple:

- take regular physical base backups
- archive WAL continuously to object storage
- use snapshots to accelerate recovery when your storage stack supports them
- restore into a new cluster, then validate before promotion

That avoids two common traps:

- treating snapshots as the whole disaster-recovery plan
- overcomplicating recovery with too many one-off scripts and manual steps

If your operator supports it, snapshot-based recovery can shorten the time needed to rehydrate large datasets. CloudNativePG, for example, supports restoring from a `VolumeSnapshot` and then applying archived WAL to reach the target time. It also warns that if you use separate WAL storage, that snapshot must be included too.

Section: What does PostgreSQL PITR on Kubernetes actually require?
At minimum, you need a recoverable base backup, continuous WAL archiving, and a tested restore workflow that can recover to a specific target time or restore point.

Point-in-time recovery (PITR) lets you restore a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster to any exact moment — the instant before a bad `DELETE`, not just last night’s snapshot. It rests on two pieces: a physical base backup taken with `pg_basebackup`, and a continuous stream of write-ahead log (WAL) segments shipped off the server by `archive_command`. To recover, you lay down the base backup, point `restore_command` at the WAL archive, set `recovery_target_time` to the moment you want, drop a `recovery.signal` file, and start the server. It replays WAL forward from the backup until it reaches your target, then stops. On PostgreSQL 15, 16, and 17 the old `recovery.conf` is gone — recovery settings live in `postgresql.auto.conf` and the presence of `recovery.signal` is what puts the server into recovery mode. The configuration is a few lines; the part that actually saves you is rehearsing the restore before you need it.

Section: Step-by-step
```
LOG:  starting point-in-time recovery to 2026-07-21 14:19:55-04
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000004" from archive
LOG:  recovery stopping before commit of transaction 1234, time 2026-07-21 14:19:56.02-04
LOG:  recovery has paused
HINT:  Execute pg_wal_replay_resume() to promote.
```
**10. Inspect, then promote.** Connect and check the data (see the next section). When satisfied, end recovery and open the cluster read-write.

`SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();`
The server finishes on a new timeline and begins accepting writes. `pg_promote()` is the equivalent when you want to force the end immediately.
